Maximum likelihood estimation in reinforcement learning (RL) is often hindered by
the issue of sparse data collection. Specifically, RL algorithms often gather
very little data in a vast action space, resulting in poor performance due to
overestimation of the Q-value for selected actions. This paper presents a novel
reward-based learning (RBL) approach that overcomes these limitations. By
redefining the target Q-value as a function of reward, RBL enables agents to
learn from past experiences and make more accurate predictions. The proposed
RBL framework is not only grounded in theoretical justification, but also
proven to significantly outperform existing methods like DQN on complex tasks. 
A comprehensive analysis of RBL highlights its benefits, including the ability to
learn without prior knowledge of the environment's dynamics and the capacity to
generalize to new situations. The study concludes that RBL offers a promising
solution to existing limitations in RL and contextual bandits, offering a
practical alternative for real-world applications. The accompanying code can be
found at https://github.com/zhengshuani/RL- RewardBiased-Learning.

While AI-assisted video editing is a promising area of research, the lack of a comprehensive dataset and thorough evaluation methods hinders progress in the field. By leveraging the quality annotations and a diverse set of datasets, we have established a robust benchmark suite that encompasses all four tasks. Furthermore, we have established new performance standards for each of the four tasks and provide in-depth analysis of the current state of AI-assisted video editing, along with a set of open challenges and potential research paths for the field. Moreover, we show that the predicted correlation functions are accurate up to an order of magnitude equal to the square root of the imaginary part of the zero in question. Brain tumor segmentation using MRI scans has become a crucial task in brain cancer diagnosis and treatment. The challenge lies in accurately identifying and isolating the tumor boundaries from the brain's surrounding tissues, as well as managing inconsistent data from various sources. To address this, we introduce a novel 3D convolutional network that incorporates contextual information to enhance segmentation accuracy. The network's encoder-decoder architecture includes a U-Net structure, which allows it to extract and integrate contextual features at multiple scales, while also learning more complex transformations through skip connections. By training on three distinct datasets - BraTS 2018, BraTS 2017, and Brain Tumor Segmentation 2016 - we demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed model in handling data with varying resolutions and modalities. Notably, our approach achieves top results in public dataset challenges, outperforming other state-of-the-art brain tumor segmentation methods. As deep learning models become increasingly prevalent in various fields,
the need to safeguard their intellectual property is becoming more pressing. This
challenge is being addressed by the introduction of watermarking techniques, which
aim to protect datasets and models by embedding robust digital signatures. However,
existing solutions to dataset watermarking are limited by their susceptibility to
attack, as they often rely on visible backdoor triggers that are easily detectable
by model defenders. To address this issue, we propose a new type of watermark,
untargeted backdoor watermark, which employs an invisible backdoor trigger to
previously protect against trigger-based attacks. This novel approach not
only maintains the integrity of watermarked models but also significantly
reduces the likelihood of being discovered by model defenders. Comprehensive
experiments conducted on multiple datasets and models demonstrate the
effectiveness and resilience of our proposed watermark, which achieves a
remarkable accuracy of 0.95 and a remarkably low rate of 1e-4 for a successful
attack. This groundbreaking work marks a significant milestone in the field of
untargeted backdoor watermarking in dataset protection. The accompanying code
for replication can be found at the following GitHub repository. 
https://github.com/ChenyangXu/UBW_Dataset_Copyright_Protection. 
With the release of this work, we anticipate a new era of dataset watermarking that
is both robust and stealthy. 
For a more detailed overview, please refer to the corresponding article published
in NeurIPS 2021. 
"Untargeted Backdoor Watermark: Towards Robust and Stealthy Dataset Copyright
Protection". 
https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.06561.

Forensic and Security. 
(https://doi.org/10.1109/TIFS, 2022). 
Additionally, this work has been presented at the 2021 IEEE Data Science Workshop

Bivectors, represented by pairs of vectors, are crucial components in various physical theories, encompassing electromagnetic fields and the Weyl tensor in Einstein's general relativity. A thorough analysis of the alpha-decay and other particle-decay processes is conducted for a series of superheavy nuclei with 122-157 atoms and 280-304 neutrons. Calculations are performed by the Gross-Burnidge-Villars potential model, adjusted for the alpha particle and its particles, to determine the alpha-decay widths. The model is coupled with the Quasi-Particle Random Phase Approximation to calculate the probabilities of particle-decay processes. The study identifies a transition zone where the alpha-decay process transitions to a stronger particle-decay process, and discovers that the neutron transfer process significantly influences the alpha-decay process, resulting in a specific decay mode for each nucleus, with either alpha-decay or neutron transfer considered the primary decay process. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through experiments on multiple benchmark datasets, which show that our method achieves state-of-the-art results while reducing computational costs. Our system's effectiveness is demonstrated through both simulated and real-world experiments, which reveal that it achieves loop closures at 99.9% and 100.0% accuracy in simulation and real scenarios, respectively. In this study, we investigate the relationship between geometric characteristics of data manifolds and how well different machine learning models perform on related tasks. Our research indicates that models with inherent robustness, such as bagging and random forests, excel in low-dimensional data manifolds, whereas models with inherent complexity, such as neural networks, perform better in high-dimensional spaces. A theoretical framework explaining this phenomenon is proposed, suggesting that models with inherent robustness excel in compact manifolds while those with inherent complexity perform better in high-quality, complex manifolds. These findings have significant implications for choosing an appropriate learning model for a given problem. Furthermore, we propose a data-driven approach to predicting a model's performance based on the manifold's geometric characteristics. To validate our proposed method, we tested it on three real-world datasets and found that it effectively predicts the performance of machine learning models. In practice, this method can aid data curators in assessing the potential performance of a dataset based on its underlying structure. Moreover, this study has important implications for understanding the behavior of neural networks, particularly in the context of adversarial robustness, suggesting that neural networks are vulnerable to attacks in compact manifolds while being more resilient in complex, high-dimensional spaces. Finally, we propose that this line of research can contribute to identifying the underlying factors causing the success and failure of neural networks in various applications. This research paper delves into the justice implications of AI-powered misinformation detection systems and their potential negative consequences. To achieve this, we examined the algorithms used in 17 high-performing systems, identified their shortcomings, and analyzed how they impact specific populations. Additionally, we investigated the algorithms' and audience's interests and power dynamics to assess potential harm. Furthermore, we discuss the stakeholders involved in these systems, their interests, and potential methods to mitigate the justice-related concerns that we've identified. Our research aims to establish a foundation for ongoing discussions on the justice implications of AI-powered misinformation detection systems. GANs have become increasingly popular for their ability to generate complex image datasets. Despite their potential, GAN training can be unreliable and difficult to navigate. One of the main issues is mode collapse, which occurs when the network becomes stuck in a limited number of patterns instead of exploring a wider variety of possibilities. This problem is often attributed to the architecture and the learning rate, but a more fundamental cause is the unstable optimization process. Our research focuses on this underlying issue, investigating how changes in Hessian eigenvalues affect mode collapse. First, we observed that mode collapse is more likely to occur when the network approaches a local minimum during training. Furthermore, we found that mode collapse is more pronounced on certain dimensions than others, suggesting that the network struggles more significantly on those coordinates. Our findings suggest that addressing mode collapse requires a thorough understanding of how changes in Hessian eigenvalues impact generator architecture, and we propose a new approach to detect mode collapse by monitoring Hessian eigenvalue fluctuations during training. Our work provides empirical evidence that mode collapse is a direct result of the unstable optimization process, and offers a new perspective on understanding GAN training. We believe that our contributions can help demystify the complex world of GAN research and provide a foundation for further advancements in the field. Deep learning models have a vulnerability that can be exploited by the Trojan horse attack, where a small portion of the model's input is manipulated to trigger a backdoor, allowing attackers to manipulate model outputs. Our research introduces a new technique called DeepPayload, a stealthy backdoor assault on deep learning models. This technique injects a malicious payload, constructed from a generative neural model, into the input, undetected by traditional Trojan horse detection methods. The injected payload is generated in a manner that minimizes the difference from the original input, making it less noticeable. Our experiments on various computer vision tasks have shown that DeepPayload can successfully trigger a backdoor with a trigger size as small as 1 pixel in a 28x28 image, achieving a high success rate. The proposed attack is particularly effective against methods that rely on distinguishing the trigger from the original input, as the malicious payload is designed to be similar. Additionally, our study demonstrates that DeepPayload can be used to create complex, high-quality triggers, making it more difficult to detect than existing Trojan horse attacks. The proposed attack is flexible and can be applied to any model that uses a generative neural model, making it a versatile tool for conducting stealthy attacks on deep learning models. Over the past decade, Dynamic Nuclear Polarization (DNP) in bulk samples at ambient temperatures has experienced significant advancements. These breakthroughs highlight the potential of diamond with Nitrogen-Void centers as a viable DNP polarization source for a variety of applications in NMR spectroscopy. Additionally, the research findings present a significant step towards the development of NMR spectroscopy capabilities at ambient conditions. Finally, the study also highlights the potential of diamond with Nitrogen-Void centers in the development of new quantum technologies.

A novel stopping point for Krylov method solvers has been proposed.  This criterion is founded on the concept of early termination based on successive estimates of residual norms, which originates from the second-order trust-region Newton method's line model.  Our results indicate that this approach yields comparable or superior performance to conventional criteria such as the sequence termination criterion and the norm ratio criterion.  Notably, we observed that our proposed criterion accelerates convergence in interior point methods used for convex quadratic programming, outperforming the norm ratio criterion and achieving a 2.8 times speedup in certain cases.  In addition, we found that our approach maintains a comparable performance to the sequence termination criterion.  This research also extends to real-time control applications where we successfully implemented our criterion in an adaptive gradient method for constrained optimization and achieved a 4 times speedup in solving time-varying linear-quadratic cost problems compared to the sequence termination criterion. Liquid metal jet additive manufacturing is an emerging 3D printing technology
that offers significant advantages over traditional methods, such as reduced
material usage and energy efficiency. However, simulating the process requires
complex modeling, which can be a significant challenge due to its computational
requirements. This study presents an innovative approach to accelerating the
simulation of liquid metal jet additive manufacturing at a part-scale level by
utilizing operator learning techniques. Initially, a comprehensive, multiscale
model was developed to simulate the LMJAM process across multiple length scales
and timescales. Following this, a deep neural network was trained to predict
the outcomes of the simulation using a small dataset of input parameters. The
results show that the neural network can accurately simulate the LMJAM process
at a part-scale level, achieving errors of less than 3% and 12% for specific
input parameters, respectively. Furthermore, the trained neural network can be
used to accelerate the simulation of the LMJAM process, enabling the analysis of
complex geometries that would be beyond computational capability using traditional
methods. This breakthrough has the potential to significantly accelerate the
design and optimization of complex geometries for LMJAM, thereby reducing the
design and fabrication cycle time. The study also highlights the potential of
operator learning in accelerating simulations across various fields and
highlighting its importance in future manufacturing advancements.

A novel dynamic feature extraction filter is introduced, leveraging the traditional logarithmic barrier function and a proposed dynamic compensation mechanism to produce an efficient and robust filtering system. The logarithmic barrier function generates a large response to abrupt time-series changes while minimizing the impact of gradual changes. The dynamic compensation mechanism further enhances this by amplifying significant sudden changes and minor step responses. The resulting filter is characterized by its efficient computation, low memory requirements, and simple implementation. The filter is applied to ECG signals, demonstrating its ability to distinguish between normal and abnormal heartbeats. The outcomes indicate that the proposed filter outperforms traditional features by offering higher accuracy and better resilience to atypical heartbeats, while also reducing the computational complexity by up to 40%. The proposed feature extraction system is suitable for real-time implementation on low-power devices due to its efficiency. The results also highlight the potential of the proposed filter to produce valuable insights for clinical applications. Sparse Mixture of Experts (MoE) models have been found to be computationally efficient and effective in NLP tasks. However, current sparse MoE models have a significant drawback in that they require the explicit activation of expert gates for each token, which can be computationally expensive. This paper proposes a solution to this issue by introducing a communication-efficient regularization method for sparse Transformers. By incorporating a dropout mechanism into the expert gate activation process, this method enables the model to learn more sparse and efficient gate structures. We evaluate our method on two widely used sparse models and find that it achieves comparable results to the original models while significantly reducing computational overhead. Moreover, our method outperforms previous sparse learning methods in terms of computational efficiency. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been successfully applied to various tasks, such as node classification and clustering, by aggregating neighborhood information for each task. However, this approach has a limitation - it relies heavily on the quality of the neighborhoods used for aggregation. This paper proposes a novel GNN solution, called NODE-SELECT, which addresses this limitation by selectively choosing high-quality neighborhoods using a discriminative process. By doing so, NODE-SELECT can potentially achieve better performance than existing GNN methods. Our experiments on four datasets have shown that NODE-SELECT outperforms other state-of-the-art GNN methods in terms of accuracy. Moreover, a comprehensive analysis of the results highlights the benefits of the NODE-SELECT framework. Notably, it demonstrates its ability to provide transparent explanations for its predictions. Our findings also reveal that a key factor contributing to NODE-SELECT's success is the diversity of the selected neighborhoods, which in turn suggests that the quality of the inductive learning process is also an important consideration. To validate this hypothesis, we conducted an additional experiment that confirms the relationship between neighborhood diversity and inductive learning quality. Overall, our research has significant implications for the development of GNNs and deep learning models in general. Our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/krishan-jyoti/NODE-SELECT. Deep learning-based monocular visual SLAM systems have shown significant potential for navigation but struggle with 3D LiDAR point clouds' complexity. To address this challenge, a novel network called AttDLNet is proposed to address the place recognition problem in LiDAR odometry. AttDLNet incorporates a LiDAR backbone and an attention-based cross-view feature extractor to identify matching features across different views. The LiDAR backbone extracts local features from individual LiDAR scans, while the attention-based module extracts cross-view features through a cross-attention mechanism. By combining these features through a fully connected layer, a correlation matrix is generated, and the most similar views are selected to update the pose estimation. A new approach to derive exact solutions of a broad class of nonlinear delay reaction-diffusion equations with variable coefficients is proposed, leveraging linear scaling and comparison method. Through identification of the stationary points and use of linear scaling, it's demonstrated that these points can be associated with solutions of the undelayed reaction-diffusion equation. Furthermore, it's established that the dynamics of delay reaction-diffusion equations around stationary points converge to that of the undelayed version, enabling the extraction of exact solutions. This comparative method is applied to the extended Fisher equation, resulting in the identification of an exponential pattern, and precise solutions of both traveling wave and logistic forms are also obtained. Notably, it's found that the delay equation may admit more solution types than its undelayed counterpart, a phenomenon illustrated by the discovery of a novel traveling wave solution of the extended Fisher equation. This study provides a general method for the exact derivation of solutions of delay reaction-diffusion equations, complementing the existing approaches in the literature. It also sheds light on the role of delay in shaping the dynamics of these equations, particularly in the enhancement of the exponential growth pattern observed in the extended Fisher equation. Moreover, it's demonstrated that the delay equation may exhibit richer dynamics than its undelayed counterpart, a characteristic that may be useful in the study of real-world systems. The findings of this study are expected to contribute to a deeper understanding of delay reaction-diffusion dynamics and inspire further research in the field. Further generalizations and refinements of the comparative method are also proposed, aiming to expand the scope of nonlinear delay reaction-diffusion equations that can be tackled using this approach. Conversational search systems often face the challenge of inaccurate or incomplete user input. This issue is particularly pronounced in multi-round conversations, where the system must effectively retrieve relevant documents despite incomplete user feedback, often in the form of brief user feedback provided within a conversational context. A proposed solution is the Keyword Extraction Transformer (KET), a neural architecture that leverages a combination of the BERT model and a temporal context encoder to predict a sequence of unmasked tokens representing potential keywords. By employing a novel loss function and incorporating a temporal context encoder, KET can accurately capture the nuances of user feedback, resulting in a more effective retrieval system. Our experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of KET, achieving a 30% reduction in recall errors compared to existing methods. Moreover, KET can be seamlessly integrated into end-to-end neural conversational systems to extract keywords, which are then utilized as query inputs for a retrieval system. This integration yields a substantial 40% improvement in the system's recall, according to experimental evaluations. Handwritten date recognition, a critical task for handwritten text analysis, involves both line and word level recognition, particularly when dealing with dates.
This paper outlines the development of the DARe system, a scaleable solution for handwritten date recognition, encompassing both the word and line-level domains.
In the 2020 HTRBDF Challenge, the proposed system secured a top position for handwritten date recognition.
This paper details the system's architecture, discusses strategies for addressing key challenges, and presents experimental findings on both training and inference phases. 
Additionally, the code, models, and dataset used for DARe are publicly accessible at https://github.com/cesarolmedo/DARe-HWDRBDF2020, enabling researchers to build on this work. 
The findings demonstrate that our proposed system excels in both line and word-level handwritten date recognition for this specific task. 
A key innovation of the DARe system lies in its ability to achieve state-of-the-art performance while maintaining a compact model size, making it suitable for edge-based applications. 
This work aims to advance the development of handwritten date recognition techniques and contribute to their practical application. 
Furthermore, the authors aim to enhance the use of Handwritten Text Analysis for real-world document analysis tasks. 
As future work, the authors plan to extend the system to process multi-line documents and develop a more generalised HTA system capable of handling various document types.

Image dehazing is a critical issue in image processing that affects visual perception and computer vision applications. Current methods either fail to utilize full image potential or are limited by their focus on local details, resulting in incomplete image information extraction. To address this, a novel framework is proposed to efficiently extract rich image features, which are then leveraged by a CNN to restore clear, high-quality images from hazy images. The proposed Feature Affinity Module (FAM) enables the network to capture both local and global image structures and global textures, while a Dual Fusion Module (DPM) aggregates local features into a global feature, providing a comprehensive image representation. The network is trained end-to-end using a combination of feature-level and image-level losses, with the DPM facilitating feature aggregation. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art dehazing performance, outperforming existing approaches in terms of PSNR, SSIM, and FAD, with source code available on GitHub.

Recent deep learning based tracking methods have achieved significant success, yet most of them rely on a fixed model trained using synthetic data and test performance on real world videos is often hindered by domain shift issues. To address this challenge, a novel dynamic learning approach is proposed, which utilizes a running buffer of real tracklets to update the model in an end-to-end fashion. This approach, referred to as DLT, enables dynamic model updates by minimizing the difference between the synthetic and real tracklets, and is shown to improve tracking performance in various challenging scenarios. Evaluations on three benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of DLT, with results indicating a notable boost in performance on OTB1, VOT2018, and LA, and a substantial reduction in localization error. Accurate long-term agricultural trends are crucial for informed decision-making, but they're often based on unreliable or imprecise data, which can lead to incorrect conclusions. Using higher-resolution satellite imagery can provide more detailed and accurate data on land use, but this data must be precise enough to be useful for decision-makers. We investigated the effectiveness of different image resolution and processing models in predicting crop production in Senegal, and found that a simple linear model using 30m data outperformed more complex models using 90m and 432m data, indicating that a relatively low-resolution image can provide sufficient precision for early trend estimates. We also found that using early-predictive machine learning models can provide a competitive alternative to traditional seasonal data, which can be especially useful during years with missing or incomplete records. Overall, our study demonstrates that early and less-precise data can provide a viable option for decision-makers, particularly in data-scarce environments. Additionally, our research data has the potential to be used in other sub-Saharan African countries with similar climate and agricultural conditions. The technology of movement sensing is becoming increasingly popular in industries such as healthcare and gaming. Movement-sensing technology offers numerous benefits, including the potential for non-invasive tracking of vital signs. Chosen for its compact size and ease of programming, the Raspberry Pi 4 has been used in the development of a motion-sensing device powered by the Pi. By leveraging the Chip Select Input/Output (CSI) camera modules, which are capable of capturing image frame noise dependent on motion, a custom-built system has successfully translated frame noise into quantitative movement patterns. Initial testing has shown promising results, with the accompanying code now making it possible for anyone to replicate the system using a Raspberry Pi 4 and two CSI cameras. DiffSVC is based on a computer algorithm that gradually transforms the features of an original voice into those of a different voice, using a process called a diffusion model. The model's structure is well-suited for voice conversion because it can be easily trained and applied to different voices, and it can also be modified to ensure that the converted voice sounds natural and authentic. When tested on a large dataset of voice recordings, DiffSVC demonstrated significant improvements over other state-of-the-art methods for voice conversion. Additionally, the model's ability to convert the tones of non-native English speakers' voices to different accents was successfully demonstrated. Overall, DiffSVC represents a significant advancement in the field of voice conversion, and it has the potential to open up new possibilities for the development of voice conversion technology. Our approach relies on a neural network that predicts the optimal camera position to achieve a desired action, based on a representation of the environment that captures its layout, object characteristics, and potential actions. which simultaneously identifies time intervals and corresponding sound events. 
This approach leverages a modified YOLOv3 architecture tailored for audio 
segmentation, utilizing a custom dataset of human-annotated sound events from 
unlabeled audio sources. By employing YOLOv3's convolutional features, 
our method efficiently identifies multiple, non-overlapping segments and their 
associated sound events. Notably, this method operates without pre-defined 
segmentation guidelines, allowing for dynamic segmentation based on the scene's 
audio context. Our results demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on the 
task of segmenting and identifying sound events from unlabeled audio sources.

segmenting and identifying sound events, animal detection, and free-word 
speech recognition. Furthermore, we make the source code and pre-trained models 
available to the public, including our YOLOv3 model, sound event detection model,

The shortest route problem is a critical optimization issue in computer vision, affecting tasks such as route optimization, resource allocation, and visual tracking. A deep neural network-based approach is proposed to estimate the distance of the shortest path between two points within an image. Our method employs a simplified neural network structure, focusing on a single convolutional block and a shared network architecture for two point-to-point estimation. We utilize the KITTI dataset to evaluate our proposed method, finding it outperforms traditional ground distance calculation and alternative deep learning-based solutions. Our approach is also extended to estimate the distance of the shortest route under the constraint of a dynamic time window. Our research aims to facilitate the development of applications such as autonomous driving, robotic path planning, and resource allocation in wireless networks. The fairness of probabilistic machine learning models is a pressing issue that requires urgent attention. In contrast to deterministic models, assessing fairness in probabilistic models is a complex challenge. Currently, there is a lack of comprehensive methods for evaluating the fairness of such models. This study aims to address this gap by developing a framework for evaluating the fairness of probabilistic models using statistical tests. By leveraging the connection between probability and statistics, our framework enables a thorough assessment of probabilistic fairness, encompassing both statistical fairness and statistical bias. Building on this foundation, we introduce a new notion of probabilistic fairness that accounts for uncertainty, and establish a systematic approach to testing for probabilistic fairness using statistical methods. Furthermore, we propose a unified framework for evaluating probabilistic fairness and develop a corresponding testing procedure. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated through its application to a range of probabilistic models, including Bayesian networks, logistic regression, and neural networks. The findings of this study are also extended to the context of causal inference, where they are expected to have a significant impact on the field. The code and supporting data for this research are publicly available on GitHub. This research is a crucial step towards ensuring the fairness of probabilistic models and promoting responsible machine learning practices. As such, it is hoped that this work will inspire future research in probabilistic fairness and motivate the development of more effective evaluation methods for probabilistic models. In contrast, a new class of transformer-based models has emerged, offering superior performance and reduced computational requirements. However, existing transformer models designed for semantic segmentation often fall short in terms of performance, particularly when compared to their convolutional counterparts. In an effort to bridge this gap, this study introduces the RTFormer, a cutting-edge transformer model engineered to excel in semantic segmentation. By combining the benefits of both convolutional and transformer models, the RTFormer features an innovative architecture that leverages a hierarchical structure and efficient real-time execution capabilities. Comprehensive evaluations conducted on various datasets demonstrate that the RTFormer not only outperforms current transformer models but also rivals state-of-the-art convolutional models. In terms of efficiency, the RTFormer boasts a speed of 20 frames per second on a single NVIDIA 2080Ti GPU, far surpassing its closest competitor. When paired with a powerful GPU, the RTFormer achieves a remarkable speed of 100 frames per second, far outpacing its closest convolutional rival by an order of magnitude. This research investigates the fluorescence properties of carbon dots (CDs) obtained from cigarette smoke, focusing on their application in bio-imaging. Cigarette smoke was purified through multiple stages to isolate CD fractions of varying sizes. The smallest CD fraction was further analyzed via transmission electron microscopy, revealing spherical particles with average diameters of 2.98 nm. The CD fractions demonstrated fluorescence in both the ultraviolet and near-infrared spectrum ranges. Notably, a fraction of CD particles exhibited a 450 nm fluorescence peak. To validate their bio-imaging potential, a cell culture experiment was conducted, where CD fractions were applied to HeLa cells prior to fixation. The results showed that incorporating CD fractions at specific concentrations prior to fixation enabled a clearer staining effect in cell membranes compared to fixed cells. The findings indicate that CD extraction from cigarette smoke may offer a low-cost, harmless bio-imaging agent. The versatility of CD fluorescence also suggests their potential for applications in bio-sensing and bio-tracking. This research provides a new perspective on repurposing cigarette smoke waste, offering a more sustainable alternative. The discovery highlights the potential benefits of repurposing CD fractions, addressing concerns surrounding smoke's negative health effects while unlocking their value as a valuable resource. This study may inspire further research into repurposing CD fractions, mitigating the environmental and health risks associated with their production, and unlocking their hidden potential. The findings of this study are expected to contribute to a deeper understanding of CD fluorescence, paving the way for innovative applications in bio-imaging and beyond. The authors hope that this research will motivate researchers to explore the repurposing of CD fractions, driving progress towards a more circular economy and a healthier, more sustainable future. We present an innovative approach to learning from demonstrations in complex environments that can effectively evaluate and enhance performance in a wide range of tasks. This method utilizes a neural network to simulate the environment and predict task success based on the agent's current state. By learning from a single demonstration, the network can determine the key states necessary for task success and then generate policy updates that improve task completion rates. This method is highly adaptable, allowing it to be applied across various domains without requiring domain-specific modifications. We successfully tested this approach on a challenging cartpole bouncing task, where a single demonstration was used to learn both state prediction and policy update models. This learning process resulted in significantly improved performance, with an average success rate of 99.7% in 80% of simulations. Notably, the method can also be applied to unseen environments, transfer learning effectively, and even refine a previously learned policy to achieve better outcomes. Additionally, the approach can effectively incorporate user feedback, leading to even more significant enhancements in task completion rates. Overall, this method offers a highly effective way to learn from demonstrations in complex environments. The associated code is available on GitHub.

The proliferation of machine learning has led to the rise of distributed machine learning, known as Federated Learning (FL), to safeguard user data privacy. However, FL's effectiveness is compromised by the disparity in data distribution among clients, leading to a decline in model performance, particularly for resource-constrained users. This phenomenon, referred to as the "inflation of loss," has a negative impact on underprivileged groups. To address this issue, we introduce a new framework, FedEArl, which prioritizes equity-awareness in FL. By leveraging a client selection strategy and a loss penalty mechanism, FedEArl aims to optimize the performance of underprivileged users. Our proposed approach is evaluated using multiple datasets and real-world applications, and the results demonstrate the efficacy of FedEArl in enhancing the performance of underprivileged groups and overall convergence of FL. Furthermore, we have conducted an in-depth analysis of the impact of various factors on the performance of underprivileged groups. Our study also identifies the limitations of existing research and provides insights for future directions in the field of Federated Learning. This work is available at https://github.com/asharakeh/FedEArl.

Predicting and preventing traffic accidents is a crucial area of study in intelligent video analysis.  The key factor in accident anticipation lies in understanding the dynamic nature of potential risks in an environment over time and space.  We propose a new approach, the Dynamic Spatial-Temporal Focus Network (D-STFN), which combines a spatio-temporal framework with a spatial attention mechanism to identify risks in real-time video footage.  D-STFN employs a strategy of non-markov temporal attention to capture long-term dependencies and incorporates a spatial attention mechanism to localize critical regions within frames.  We demonstrate that D-STFKB outperforms existing methods in accuracy on three public datasets, specifically eITPKT, Real-world Traffic Accident, and APTOS, with state-of-the-art results on APTOS.  Our approach also outperforms the baseline method in an e-commerce setting, the Linx dataset, and achieves competitive results with a more complex model. The reliability of electricity transmission networks relies on the balance between supply and demand to maintain frequency stability. A slight imbalance between these elements leads to instantaneous price fluctuations, influencing consumer behavior and driving market trading. This research examines the impact of trading on grid frequency fluctuations, using data from the Nordic market integration zone between 2011 and 2014. A frequency-fluctuation model is developed, incorporating trading moments and geo-political factors, to gauge the trading's influence on frequency stability. Results indicate that trading has a significant effect on frequency fluctuations, with price-based trading increasing amplitude by 30% and time-based trading by 10%. Moreover, price trading amplifies fluctuations in countries with more extensive market integration, whereas time trading is more pronounced in those with weaker integration. This study highlights the need for further research into the trading's impact on grid frequency stability, particularly in regions with weak connections, facilitating better network control and governance. In this study, we focus on enhancing the performance of solutions to Constrained Markov Decision Processes through a new approach called the Constrained Policy Iteration (CPI). This method iteratively generates a set of policies that meet the constraints and then selects the best one for the current state distribution. Building upon previous research, we developed the two-sided policy improvement theorem to analyze the efficiency of the CPI algorithm. Our key contribution includes a novel variant of this theorem that guarantees a rapid global convergence when the optimal Q-function is continuous. Two long-standing problems of Alfred Menger have been resolved. First, a 
proof is provided for a conjecture made by Menger in 1932 that, in Euclidean space, 
any two non-parallel planes can be linked by a series of planes that together 
cover the space and entirely separate points A and B. Second, a 1926 question 
posed by Menger about the possibility of a flat structure in three-dimensional 
space is answered negatively by constructing an object that cannot be flat in such 
a space. This construction builds on earlier work by Menger and a 2005 object 
created by Brian Clutworthy. Key concepts and results from Menger's work are 
summarized, alongside the construction methods used for the proofs. Additionally, 
a third problem related to Menger's work has been identified and partially 
solved, and a portion of this solution is provided. It is also noted that certain 
of the Euclidean space's properties can be applied to other types of metric spaces. 
A final observation is made about the applicability of a flat structure in four 
dimensional space.

A novel cooperative adaptive cruise control system, leveraging a stochastic model predictive control approach, is developed to optimize traffic flow and reduce traffic congestion. The proposed method uses a Gaussian Process to forecast the trajectory of the front vehicle in a platoon, incorporating both policy-dependent and platoon-dependent variables. By minimizing total braking costs, an optimal control policy is derived through stochastic optimization. Simulation results demonstrate a 10-20% decrease in platoon delay and 5-10% reduction in total braking energy compared to a centralized greedy method. Additionally, the method exhibits improved robustness to non-recurring traffic disturbances and outperforms other methods in realistic scenarios. The proposed method's computational efficiency enables real-time application in cooperative vehicle control systems. Overall, the method's ability to optimize traffic behavior and reduce energy consumption makes it an attractive solution for real-world traffic management. immediate and life-saving care during medical emergencies. The COVID-19 pandemic
has placed considerable strain on EMS services, prompting a need to address
the unexpected increase in calls. This study aims to predict EMS calls in New
York City by leveraging open data sources, specifically focusing on hospital
trends, to develop a predictive model that can anticipate EMS calls ahead of time. Our
analysis, which covers a period from March to May 2020, shows that using
hospitalization trends, we can accurately forecast EMS calls with a notable
correlation coefficient of 0.811. The results also indicate that our model can
extend its predictions to future days, specifically up to one day in advance. By
analyzing EMS calls in relation to hospitalization rates and comparing our
findings to those from other cities, we aim to contribute to the ongoing efforts
to mitigate the burden on EMS services during the COVID-19 pandemic. Our
research has significant implications for the development of predictive tools that
can help prepare EMS personnel for an increasingly demanding situation. Ultimately,
our work seeks to provide a data-driven framework that can be scaled up to create
predictive models for EMS calls across the United States. This research was presented

Phase noise causes frequency-domain correlations between different subcarriers, making it challenging to mitigate it by removing subcarriers with high correlations. Our research shows that phase noise correlations can actually be utilized to detect targets in OFDM monostatic radars by exploiting the fact that they are non-Gaussian and exhibit a specific correlation pattern. We have developed a new detection statistic that can take advantage of this non-Gaussianity to further improve detection performance. Our simulation results confirm that this approach outperforms both the standard signal-to-noise ratio statistic and a previous method that removed correlated subcarriers, especially in low-SNR conditions and for longer pulse lengths. Furthermore, our research highlights the importance of carefully designing the pulse length and number of subcarriers in OFDM monostatic radars to ensure optimal performance. Our findings also indicate that phase noise can be a useful feature in deep learning-based radar detection tasks, and we provide a dataset for further research. This paper explores the long-term behavior of a two-dimensional chemotaxis model, incorporating a singular chemotactic sensitivity and the logistic source term, which is shown to have global classical solutions of positive bounds through the use of the Lyapunov functional approach. By establishing the uniform estimates for the solutions and their derivatives, we demonstrate the convergence of the solutions and their gradients towards certain mean-field solutions within the framework of the Lyapunov functional framework, ultimately proving the existence of a global attractor for the system and showing that it is a weak Scott--Zachary system with certain properties. We also show that this system has a compact attractor and that its trajectory attractor is unique on this attractor, while an initial value problem with large initial conditions is analyzed, demonstrating the existence of a strong solution that is unique and continuous in time and remains bounded for all positive times. Furthermore, we derive the existence of a pullback attractor for the system and show that it is pathwise asymptotically stable. Finally, the results are compared with existing literature. Our proposed model incorporates a unique fusion module that combines video and audio information to make accurate predictions. The rapid growth of IoT devices has led to a significant increase in data collection, storage, and computation needs, posing a challenge to network bandwidth and computational capacity. To address this issue, offloading computations from devices to servers has become a viable solution, yet it often relies on expensive and complex server-side infrastructure. Our research focuses on self-service offloading, a novel approach that allows personal devices to offload computations to IoT edge servers using standard hardware, eliminating the need for sophisticated and costly server-side infrastructure. By giving users control over the offloading process, they can decide when and which computations to offload, and how to optimize the process. Our experimental results demonstrate that self-service offloading can achieve comparable performance to traditional server-side offloading, with only a 1.6x increase in communication overhead. The goal of Visual Question Answering (VQA) is to accurately respond to open-ended visual queries. Domain-specific VQA models, which excel on specific datasets but struggle on others, are a common challenge. The lack of generalization in VQA models is due to differences in training and test data, necessitating a novel approach. We present the RAMEN framework, an adaptation of the MSTR method, to address domain generalization in VQA by separating object identification and answer generation. RAMEN's object identification module uses a contrastive learning technique to generate robust visual representations, while its answer generation module utilizes zero-shot transfer learning to generate accurate answers. RAMEN's object identification module is effective in object recognition tasks and can be easily integrated with other VQA approaches to enhance their performance. In recent years, the field of film recognition has gained significant attention,
driven by the growing number of user-generated videos on platforms like YouTube,
and the increasing importance of copyright issues for media companies. While prior
research focused on visual and audio characteristics, we propose that incorporating
textual data can greatly enhance film recognition capabilities, and thus, explore
the potential of multi-modal learning in this area. Specifically, we examine the
utility of a simple text-based film classifier, which has been overlooked in film
recognition research, and demonstrate its performance in this new context. Our
experiments reveal that the film classifier can be adapted to film recognition with
minimal training, and that it can also be improved by leveraging large-scale vision
and vision-text model pre-training. Moreover, we demonstrate that the film classifier
can be used as a starting point for multi-modal learning and that its performance in
film recognition can be improved by incorporating text data. Our results are made
available online for further reference. Finally, we discuss the limitations of the
text-based approach and suggest potential future research directions. For more
information, please visit: https://filmrecognition.github.io/. \textit{This paper

Our research presents a novel, multi-task sequence forecasting framework that addresses this problem by leveraging data from Tunisian Arabic speakers. This approach involves training models to perform multiple tasks: predicting individual characters, predicting character classes, and predicting normalised characters. We have also developed a dataset containing 12,000 unique Arabizi characters and their corresponding equivalent Unicode characters. Furthermore, we propose a pre-processing method that standardises text and transforms raw keyboard input data. This data is then used to train our model, which is evaluated on both known and unseen data to assess its effectiveness. The results demonstrate that our model can effectively predict both character classes and normalised characters, as well as translate raw keyboard input into corresponding Unicode characters with high accuracy. Moreover, we show that our model can learn from user behavior data and adapt to unseen characters, making it a promising solution for Arabizi-to-Arabic conversion. Accurate estimation of regional brain connectivity from blood oxygen level dependent signals is crucial for understanding various neurological disorders. However, current methods have limitations stemming from two main sources: the inherent biases of local connectivity estimates and the oversimplification of long-distance connections. To address these issues, a novel approach is introduced that combines spatial and temporal information to produce more reliable connectivity estimates. This method leverages spatial priors to produce region-specific BOLD times series, and then employs graph theoretical analysis on these regions to produce the final functional connectivity matrix. Through simulations and real data analysis, it is shown that this approach outperforms previous methods in reducing noise and enhancing the accuracy of regional connectivity estimates, leading to more realistic and informative results. This method's ability to produce more accurate and meaningful connectivity maps may be particularly useful in neurodegenerative disease research where disease-specific network patterns are distinct. Furthermore, this approach can be easily adapted to other neuroimaging applications requiring regional connectivity estimates. We present SynthCity, a comprehensive dataset comprising 100,000 synthetic point clouds with detailed annotations for training segmentation networks to identify 50 different categories. Each point cloud in the dataset is 10,000 pixels in size and has 50 distinct labels. We examine the effectiveness of cutting-edge segmentation networks on this scale and conduct a thorough analysis of their ability to generalize to large point clouds. Our experiments reveal that state-of-the-art networks struggle with generalization when faced with larger point clouds. We also introduce a novel metric, mean average precision per category, to assess their ability to segment individual classes. Finally, we examine the influence of oversampling smaller point clouds and find that it can lead to improved performance but also introduces bias. A critical issue in quantum information processing is controlling complex quantum systems with numerous degrees of freedom. The results show that the proposed method can efficiently produce near-optimal control policies that may be infeasible using traditional methods. Moreover, the local policy network can be successfully distributed, even among a large number of systems, indicating its potential for widespread use in quantum information processing applications. The framework's open-source implementation enables researchers to easily adapt it to various quantum control tasks, and the experimental results highlight its promising capabilities. Additionally, we show that our approach can be adapted to use other types of checkpoints, such as those from ensemble models and Hessian-based models. This involves refining the input call graphs, identifying core components of these graphs, and utilizing established software metrics to derive meaningful results. Our implementation is integrated with Rigi, a system for analyzing large software systems, where we have successfully applied CP analytics to several real-world software systems, yielding promising results. Our analysis also reveals various challenges and limitations that must be addressed moving forward. This research is significant as it is the first comprehensive study to conduct CP analytics on large-scale software systems, including the first results from the MuNet system, containing over 8 million call graphs extracted from over 1.3 million C++ lines of code. In computer vision, the task of image decomposition is crucial for multiple applications, but current deep learning-based techniques often struggle with inconsistent results. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel approach called Semi-Supervised StyleGAN for image separation. Our method leverages the stylegan generator, which we modify by decoupling the common latent code and producing multiple independent components. To optimize the separation process, we incorporate a contrastive loss and a domain loss - a novel penalty that improves domain-specific quality in an unsupervised framework. Our experiments show that the proposed method excels state-of-the-art baselines in image decomposition, as evaluated on the challenging ILSVRC2012 and CIFAR-10 datasets. Moreover, we demonstrate that our approach can adapt to new, unseen datasets without requiring any additional supervision. Our code is publicly available on GitHub. For further information, visit our project website at https://separations.github.io/. Our research is backed by a solid theoretical foundation, as detailed in the accompanying paper. Our results are the first to achieve state-of-the-art performance in image separation using an unsupervised method, opening up new opportunities for a wide range of applications. Hyperspectral images are highly valued for their potential to deliver detailed information, but they often suffer from low transmission rates and the degradation inherent to image acquisition equipment, resulting in poor quality images. Current methods for hyper-spectral image denoising have primarily focused on individual spectral bands, failing to utilize the full potential of the data. This paper proposes a novel approach that tackles hyper-spectral image denoising by leveraging spatial-spectral relationships. It introduces a network architecture, SSCAN, consisting of a spectral focus module and a spatial-spectral cross focus module. The module utilizes a cross attention mechanism to integrate information from neighboring bands. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this proposed method on three datasets, yielding superior performance over existing benchmarks. This approach utilizes a particle filter framework to predict the mixture weights and the component density functions simultaneously. Our proposed method demonstrates comparable performance to other parametric methods in a simulation study. Furthermore, we successfully applied this approach to a real-world dataset and found it to be an effective tool in identifying diverse distribution types among mixture components. Our study provides a nonparametric method for estimating a multivariate mixing distribution, which can be a useful alternative to parametric methods and may also serve as a basis for a more comprehensive nonparametric clustering solution in the future. In multi-agent reinforcement learning, a common strategy is to use a greedy approach, selecting the best action for each agent at each time step without considering potential long-term benefits. This paper reveals that this greedy approach, or the satisficing policy, can be effective in multi-agent settings. We demonstrate that under certain conditions, including uncertainty about the environment and other agents' behavior, the satisficing policy may outperform more optimistic methods, such as maximin strategies, even in situations where no dominant strategy exists. We also provide a method to determine when the satisficing policy becomes less desirable and show that this happens if the other possible approaches consistently yield better outcomes than the satisficing policy. We then discuss how the introduction of communication among agents can lead to cooperation and improve collective performance, especially in environments with uncertain outcomes, by creating opportunities for cooperation through communication channels. Finally, our results are validated through a series of simulations in games with multiple agents, including the security dilemma and the battle of the sexes. Our findings suggest that this approach may be useful in designing automatic negotiation systems and security strategies for uncertain multi-agent environments. The sunspot number series represents a fundamental aspect of solar research and a critical reference point for space weather forecasting. We introduce a new method for analyzing the dynamics of kinetically constrained models (KCMs), which allows us to derive exact equations for the temporal variations of order parameters in these systems. Our approach is based on the concept of a local effective Hamiltonian, which can be used to explain the dynamics of Mott potentials in KCMs. By considering the effects of a local effective Hamiltonian on the dynamics of particles in a system, we can derive expressions for the time-derivative of order parameters. Notably, our results for the $A_k$ model on a $d=1$ lattice match recent numerical findings by Keith Nichols. Our approach provides insight into the dynamics of KCMs and may be applied to other systems, such as the $A_3$ model and interacting particle systems. We hope that this work will inspire further research into KCMs and contribute to the development of a unified theoretical framework for understanding their dynamics. The accompanying source code is available online at https://github.com/keithnichols/kcm_dynamic_equations.

Our experiments demonstrate that this approach achieves competitive results with state-of-the-art methods using image data, and outperforms them using estimated depth maps. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) and similar methods have gained popularity for solving complex differential equations, but their practical applications are hindered by the lack of a systematic approach to ensure reliable results. To address this issue, we developed a universal framework to evaluate the effectiveness of PINNs and other algorithms when solving a wide range of differential equation systems. We designed a set of test cases with varying levels of difficulty and noise to assess how well different methods perform. We created a system to automatically generate these test cases and evaluated the performance of multiple algorithms, including traditional and physics-informed methods. Our results show that traditional methods struggle with noisy data, while physics-informed methods excel, but exhibit unstable behavior in systems with high complexity. We also discovered that combining multiple neural networks can improve stability, but at the cost of increased training time. Our findings highlight the need for more robust and efficient methods to solve real-world differential equation problems. The research and associated test cases are publicly available on GitHub. We hope that our work will facilitate the development of reliable evaluation criteria for solving complex differential equation problems. Current neural video compression models are limited by high computational demands, which hinder their practical use. To address this, we developed Gemino, a neural video compression system that significantly outperforms existing solutions in terms of PSNR and VMAF metrics while maintaining comparable computational efficiency. Key innovations include a novel wavelet domain-based network design, an efficient pixel feature fusion module, and a lossy luminance-chroma separation approach. Evaluations on multiple datasets across various quality settings confirm Gemino's superiority over current state-of-the-art methods, offering a 2-4 times improvement in terms of VMAF and PSNR metrics at equivalent encoding bitrate. Furthermore, Gemino's design allows for seamless integration with legacy HEVC-based systems, making it an attractive solution for large-scale deployment in video conferencing applications. To facilitate widespread adoption, we will make our model and pre-trained weights publicly available. A comprehensive implementation of Gemino is also planned for future work. This underestimation can be attributed to the initial assumptions of a spherically collapsing remnant. Our results also reveal that the final outcome is heavily dependent on the presence of a magnetar seed. Furthermore, we found that the final remnant of a neutron star merger can be significantly affected by the initial mass of the neutron star, with a higher initial mass leading to a higher final remnant mass. To bridge this gap, we introduce a new pre-training method that leverages both the structure and semantics of Chinese to enhance multimodal representation learning. Our approach, known as Chinese video and language pre-training (CVLP), employs a contrastive learning framework that effectively captures the complex relationships between Chinese video and language. CVLP also incorporates a unique hierarchical self-supervised learning strategy to improve the representation of fine-grained Chinese video and language elements. The task of open-set identification aims to determine whether a test sample originates from a known class or falls outside the labeled class dataset. OAI is a critical problem in unsupervised domain adaptation and detection tasks, but it is often approached as a classification problem within a supervised framework. However, this method has limitations, as it fails to account for samples that are close to the boundary between the known classes and the out-of-distribution area. In this study, we present an innovative OAI framework that leverages similarity metrics to model the proximity between a test sample and the training data. Our proposed method, A-SL, utilizes an embedding space learned via a similarity metric to identify unknown samples. We utilize an augmentation-based similarity metric to ensure that the distance between the known classes is consistently greater than the distance to the out-of-distribution area. We also introduce a novel loss function that encourages the distance between the known classes and the out-of-distribution area to be consistently smaller than a predetermined threshold. Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method, A-SL, which achieves state-of-the-art performance in open-set identification tasks.
